  Answering your two questions

  1. "If I start the program with sudo does it actually let the RF through?"

  Yes for the permissions blocker, with an important caveat about safety:

  The reason RF was blocked before was purely capability-based, not code-based.
  Your shell's effective capabilities are empty (CapEff: 0000000000000000) even
  though the bounding set contains cap_net_admin and cap_net_raw. That's why iw 
  dev wlan1 set type monitor returned "Operation not permitted" and pcap capture
  failed. Running as root gives a full capability set, so those would now
  succeed.

  But the antenna guard becomes the only thing standing between wlan1 and 
  destruction. Previously the "Operation not permitted" was accidentally doing
  the safety work. I verified the guard is real and correctly ordered:

  - code/base/utils.cpp:690 — radio_utils_set_interface_frequency() checks
    radio_cap_card_model_allows_frequency() before the iw dev ... set freq
    command
  - code/base/utils.cpp:847 — same check in
    radio_utils_set_interface_frequency_and_bandwidth(), also before tuning
  - code/base/radio_profiles.cpp:810 — radio_profiles_configure_interface()
    refuses before the monitor-mode change, so wlan1 is never even put into
    monitor mode on a 2.4 GHz profile
  - code/base/radio_capabilities.cpp:373 — wlan1's USB ID bda:881a maps to
    CARD_MODEL_RTL8812AU_DUAL_ANTENNA, which radio_cap_card_model_is_5ghz_only()
    returns true for, and the 2.4 GHz bands (23/24/25) are refused

  So the guard is load-bearing and correctly placed. The one gap I found:
  hardware_initialize_radio_interface() (called at startup from
  r_initradio.cpp:144) sets the interface to managed mode and applies datarates
  but does not tune a frequency, so it does not endanger the card.

  Recommendation: run as root, but do not select a 2.4 GHz profile for wlan1 —
  the code will refuse it, and you should trust the refusal and not work around
  it.

  2. Your SIGSEGV — that's a real bug I should fix.

  The crash is not related to RF. sudo drops XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (and
  WAYLAND_DISPLAY), so SDL's video init fails:

  error: XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is invalid or not set in the environment.

  SDL2 on Wayland needs XDG_RUNTIME_DIR to reach the compositor socket. Under
  sudo, XDG_RUNTIME_DIR isn't passed through, so SDL_Init(SDL_INIT_VIDEO) fails.
  The code at code/renderer/render_engine_desktop.cpp:84 only logs that failure
  and continues:

  if (SDL_Init(SDL_INIT_VIDEO) < 0) {
     log_softerror_and_alarm("[RenderEngineDesktop] SDL_Init failed: %s",
  SDL_GetError());
  } else { ... }

  Then initWindow() fails, initEngine() returns false — but render_init_engine()
  at code/renderer/render_engine.cpp:75 ignores that return value, so
  g_pRenderEngine is a half-constructed object with m_pCairoCtx == NULL, and the
  first cairo call dereferences NULL → SIGSEGV.

  This is a small, contained fix. Let me handle it along with the test work.

      274 +// Same as _split_annexb_nals(), but for the 4 byte start code
          +s (00 00 00 01).                                              
      275 +// The empty NAL units (a start code immediately followed by a
          +nother start                                                  
      276 +// code) are skipped. The recorded stream starts with a 4 byte
          + start code                                                   
      277 +// written by the station code, followed by the received strea
          +m, so the first                                               
      278 +// NAL unit of the recorded stream is the first NAL unit of th
          +e stream.                                                     
      279 +static int _split_annexb_nals4(const u8* pData, int iSize, int
          +* pOffsets, int* pSizes, int iMaxNals)                        
      280 +{                                                             
      281 +   int iCount = 0;                                            
      282 +   int iPos = 0;                                              
      283 +   while ( iPos + 4 <= iSize )                                
      284 +   {                                                          
      285 +      if ( pData[iPos] == 0 && pData[iPos+1] == 0 && pData[iPo
          +s+2] == 0 && pData[iPos+3] == 1 )                             
      286 +      {                                                       
      287 +         int iStart = iPos + 4;                               
      288 +         int iNext = iStart;                                  
      289 +         while ( iNext + 4 <= iSize )                         
      290 +         {                                                    
      291 +            if ( pData[iNext] == 0 && pData[iNext+1] == 0 && p
          +Data[iNext+2] == 0 && pData[iNext+3] == 1 )                   
      292 +               break;                                         
      293 +            iNext++;                                          
      294 +         }                                                    
      295 +         int iEnd = iNext;                                    
      296 +         while ( iEnd > iStart && pData[iEnd-1] == 0 )        
      297 +            iEnd--;                                           
      298 +                                                              
      299 +         if ( (iEnd > iStart) && (iCount < iMaxNals) )        
      300 +         {                                                    
      301 +            pOffsets[iCount] = iStart;                        
      302 +            pSizes[iCount] = iEnd - iStart;                   
      303 +            iCount++;                                         
      304 +         }                                                    
      305 +         iPos = iNext;                                        
      306 +         continue;                                            
      307 +      }                                                       
      308 +      iPos++;                                                 
      309 +   }                                                          
      310 +   return iCount;                                             
      311 +}

  launched with `-debug` or from pts/0.**
  - **`/RUBY_STARTED_SEMAPHORE` must not exist**:
  `sem_open("/RUBY_STARTED_SEMAPHORE", O_CREAT | O_EXCL, S_IWUSR|S_IRUSR, 0)`
  `:826`. On failure (already exists) and not debug → prints *"Ruby (v …) is
  starting..."*, `sleep(8)`, `return 0` (`:827-833`). **There is no
  `sem_unlink()` for this semaphore anywhere in the tree** (the only reference
  is `:826`; `sem_close` at `:2164`/`:2292` does not remove the named object). ⇒
  **A second `ruby_start` invocation on the same boot always takes the "already
  starting" branch and exits after 8 s.**
  - Writable `/tmp/ruby/...` tree.
  - Radio enumeration must not hang (no hard requirement on desktop).

  ### (d) What is stubbed/unsupported on desktop
  - **The entire controller spawn branch is compiled out** (`:2057-2148`) →
  desktop `ruby_start` spawns **only** `ruby_logger` (`:887`) and `ruby_start
  -initradio` (`:1995`). `ruby_controller` is **never** started; `ruby_central`
  is therefore never started either.
  - `ruby_initdhcp` not started (`:1692-1694`).
  - `_check_files()` skipped (`:1133-1135`).
  - Desktop build has **no logger service daemon**:
  `_log_check_for_service_log_access()` returns 0 immediately for
  `HW_PLATFORM_LINUX_GENERIC` (`code/base/base.c:412-417`). Yet `ruby_start`
  still spawns `ruby_logger` (`:887`) — a **useless/orphan process** on desktop;
  all desktop processes log straight to the file.
  - `renice` is skipped on desktop (`code/base/hardware_procs.cpp:2101-2106`).

  ### (e) Reachable?
  **Partially.** `ruby_start` itself is reachable (build target + it is the
  documented entry point), but on desktop it **cannot start the application**:
  it launches `ruby_logger` and a self-`initradio` child, then falls into the
  controller verification loop `:2233-2272`, where
  `ruby_central`/`ruby_controller`/`ruby_rt_station` are all absent. Note `bool
  bAllOk = false;` at `:2240` is **never set to true** (each check assigns
  `bAllOk = false`), so `if (bAllOk) break;` at `:2266` can never fire → the
  loop always runs its full **10 × 2 s = 20 s** and then `ruby_start` exits with
  code 0. Net effect on desktop: *"Ruby is starting…" → 20 s of error spam →
  exit*, with no UI.

  ---

  `IPC_CHANNEL_TYPE_ROUTER_TO_TELEMETRY` and write end of `TELEMETRY_TO_ROUTER`
  (`:735-745`). **Any failure → `return -1` (`:786-787`) — the only hard exit.**
  Serial telemetry is optional: ports not flagged `SERIAL_PORT_USAGE_DATA_LINK`
  / `SERIAL_PORT_USAGE_TELEMETRY` leave FDs at -1 and those read blocks are

  - (d) Data path: **not UDP, not shared memory** — it is a **System V message
  queue**. `try_read_messages_from_router()` `:867` (def `:417-516`) reads from
  the router over `ROUTER_TO_TELEMETRY` and handles
  `PACKET_TYPE_AUX_DATA_LINK_DOWNLOAD` `:509`,
  `PACKET_TYPE_TELEMETRY_RAW_DOWNLOAD` `:511`, `PACKET_TYPE_RC_TELEMETRY`
  `:513`. The watchdog and RC-downstream shared memories (`:814`) are used only
  for *statistics*, not for the data stream.

  (`launchers_controller.cpp:136-145`); the router (`ruby_rt_station`) must be
  the peer that feeds the queue.
  - Shutdown `:885-911`: close serial FDs `:887-893`, `ruby_close_ipc_channel()`
  `:895-896`, USB socket `:900-901`, shm closes `:906-907`.

  ## 6. Supporting processes and the stub-binary inventory

  ### IPC transport
  `RUBY_USES_MSGQUEUES 1` (`code/base/ruby_ipc.c:46`); the FIFO variant
  `RUBY_USE_FIFO_PIPES` is **commented out** at `:45`.
  `ruby_init_ipc_channels()` `:196` creates FIFOs only for Pi/Radxa
  (`:198-220`); on desktop it is effectively a no-op and the msgqueues are
  created lazily by `msgget(key, IPC_CREAT|…)` (`:326`, `:415`). Channel
  constants: `code/base/ruby_ipc.h:5-12`. `ruby_central` deletes all channels on
  start (`ruby_central.cpp:2867`).

  ### `ruby_player_desktop` — main at
  `code/r_player/ruby_player_desktop.cpp:655`
  GStreamer-based decoder; options `-p` / `-sm` / `-file` / `-h265` / `-endexit`
  / `-fps` / `-af` / `-rawp` (`:677-721`). It is the desktop replacement for
  `VIDEO_PLAYER_PIPE` / `VIDEO_PLAYER_SM` / `VIDEO_PLAYER_OFFLINE`
  (`code/base/config_file_names.h:251-253`). Built by `Makefile:333`, included
  in the desktop `station` target `:249`. **Reachable** — it is launched by
  `ruby_rt_station`'s video output (`code/r_station/rx_video_output.cpp:266`)
  and by `ruby_central`'s intro playback (`ruby_central.cpp:2846`).

  ### `ruby_video_proc` — main at `code/r_utils/ruby_video_proc.cpp:305`
  Built for desktop (`Makefile:259,281`) but on desktop is only used to
  finalize/store a leftover temp recording (spawned at `ruby_central.cpp:1984`).
  **Not required** by the desktop `r_check_processes_filesystem()`
  (`:1356-1382`).

  ### `ruby_logger` — spawned by `ruby_start` at `:887` (and `:491/:496` in the
  test path)
  **Effectively useless on desktop**: the desktop build has no logger service
  daemon and every process writes directly to the log file
  (`code/base/base.c:412-417`). It is still spawned → an orphan process on
  desktop.

  ### `ruby_i2c` — built (`Makefile:239,266`) but **never started on desktop**
  (`launchers_controller.cpp:296-302`).

  ### `ruby_tx_rc` — built (`Makefile:249,306`) but **never started on desktop**
  (`launchers_controller.cpp:165-169`).

  ### Stub binaries — expected-missing inventory
  - **`ruby_capture_stub`** — `code/base/config_file_names.h:250` (`#define
  VIDEO_RECORDER_COMMAND "ruby_capture_stub"` for desktop). Referenced by the
  **vehicle**-side video source (`code/r_vehicle/video_source_csi.cpp:206,208`;
  `code/r_vehicle/ruby_rx_commands.cpp:1608,1617`). **There is no Makefile rule,
  no source file, and no built binary for it anywhere in the tree** ⇒
  **expected-missing by design** (it is the desktop placeholder for Pi's
  `majestic` recorder, `config_file_names.h:213`). It only affects the vehicle
  path, which desktop never takes.
  - **`ruby_player_stub` — does not exist.** No Makefile rule, no source, no
  reference in the tree. The desktop equivalent is the real
  `ruby_player_desktop` (`config_file_names.h:251-253`, `Makefile:333,198-199`).
  - **`ruby_video_proc_stub` — does not exist.** `ruby_video_proc` is a real,
  built binary (`Makefile:281`, main at `code/r_utils/ruby_video_proc.cpp:305`);
  no stub variant is referenced anywhere.
  - **`ruby_capture_stub` is the only stub-named artifact in the repository.**

  ## 7. Ranked list of what is genuinely missing / broken on desktop

  1. **`ruby_start` never starts the UI on desktop.** The whole controller
  branch is `#if defined(HW_PLATFORM_RASPBERRY) || defined(HW_PLATFORM_RADXA)`
  (`code/r_start/ruby_start.cpp:2057-2148`); `hw_execute_ruby_process(NULL,
  "ruby_controller", …)` is at `:2146` inside it. Since `ruby_controller` is the
  only spawner of `ruby_central` (`code/r_station/ruby_controller.cpp:110`),
  the entire UI chain is unreachable from the entry point. ⇒ **Missing: a
  desktop branch that spawns `ruby_controller` (or `ruby_central` directly).**
  2. **Console gate blocks the desktop terminal.** `_step_find_console()`
  accepts only `/dev/tty1`, `/dev/pts/0` or `-debug` (`:789-794`); OpenIPC has
  an override (`:806-813`) but LINUX_GENERIC has none → abort at `:815-822`. ⇒
  **Missing: a desktop override.**
  3. **Start semaphore is never unlinked.** `sem_open(..., O_CREAT|O_EXCL, ...)`
  `:826`; no `sem_unlink` for `/RUBY_STARTED_SEMAPHORE` anywhere ⇒ a second
  `ruby_start` on the same boot always hits *"Ruby is starting…"* + `sleep(8)` +
  exit (`:827-833`). ⇒ **Missing: `sem_unlink` on exit.**
  4. **`bAllOk` is never set true** in the controller verification loop
  (`ruby_start.cpp:2240`, assignments at `:2243,2250,2257`, test at `:2266`) ⇒
  the 10 × 2 s retry loop always runs to completion (20 s) even when everything
  is fine.
  5. **`ruby_tx_rc` is unconditionally disabled on desktop**
  (`launchers_controller.cpp:163-169`) — even when a serial radio is present, RC
  cannot reach the vehicle.
  6. **`ruby_i2c` is unconditionally disabled on desktop**
  (`launchers_controller.cpp:296-302`), and GPIO/I2C/IONICE capabilities are
  undefined (`code/base/config_hw.h:39-53`).
  7. **Router and telemetry are gated on radio hardware**:
  `launchers_controller.cpp:56-65,70-79,136-145` and the pairing gate
  `ruby_central.cpp:2131-2135` + `code/r_central/pairing.cpp:77-82`. Without a
  serial SiK/ELRS radio, **no link process runs at all** on desktop.
  8. **The logger daemon is spawned but unused**: `ruby_start.cpp:887` spawns
  `ruby_logger`, but the desktop build bypasses the logger service
  (`code/base/base.c:412-417`).
  9. **`controller_wait_for_stop_all()` waits on a non-existent process name**
  `"ruby_rt_router"` (`launchers_controller.cpp:344`) — the real binary is
  `ruby_rt_station`.
  10. **`ruby_capture_stub` is referenced but does not exist**
  (`code/base/config_file_names.h:250`) — expected-missing; only affects the
  vehicle-side recording path.
  11. **Binary-consistency checking is skipped on desktop** (`_check_files()` is
  Pi/Radxa-only, `ruby_start.cpp:1133-1135`), and `FOLDER_BINARIES` is
  `/tmp/ruby/bin/` while the Makefile emits binaries to the repo root — so
  `hw_get_ruby_process_full_path()` only resolves them CWD-relative
  (`code/base/hardware_procs.cpp:1348-1392`).
  12. **Desktop render engine is the hard failure point for `ruby_central`**: no
  display ⇒ `render_init_engine()` returns NULL ⇒ exit 1
  (`ruby_central.cpp:2793-2800`; SDL failure messages in
  `code/renderer/render_engine_desktop.cpp:85-90,172,182,205,212,244,251`).
  13. **Camera is always absent on desktop**
  (`code/base/hardware_camera.cpp:126,150-152`), so desktop is always
  "controller" unless `FILE_FORCE_VEHICLE_NO_CAMERA` is created
  (`code/base/hardware.cpp:254-260`).
  14. **Desktop `ruby_start` runs an unnecessary `ruby_start -initradio` child**
  (`:1995`) whose result (`hardware_load_radio_info()`) is only meaningful for
  the monitor-mode NIC path.

  ## 8. Net startup chain on desktop (as the code actually behaves)

  ```
  ruby_start  (main: code/r_start/ruby_start.cpp:1503)
   ├─ console gate  :789-794 / abort :815-822          → aborts unless -debug or
  pts/0 or tty1
   ├─ /RUBY_STARTED_SEMAPHORE (O_EXCL) :826            → aborts on 2nd run
   ├─ ruby_logger                      :887            → spawned, but unused
  (base.c:412-417)
   ├─ ruby_start -initradio            :1995           → spawned
   ├─ controller branch  #if Pi||Radxa :2057-2148      → COMPILED OUT ⇒ no
  ruby_controller
   └─ verify loop :2233-2272 (bAllOk never true)       → 20 s of errors, exit 0

  (never started on desktop)  ruby_controller :110 → ruby_central →
  ruby_rt_station / ruby_rx_telemetry
  ```

  Manual-only path today: run `./ruby_central` by hand (needs CWD=build dir for
  `res/`, and a working SDL2 display) → it reaches `ruby_central.cpp:2131`; with
  a serial radio attached it will additionally start `ruby_rt_station` and
  `ruby_rx_telemetry` (and still never `ruby_tx_rc`).

  ## 1. The link layer: it is the RADIO, not UDP and not shared memory

  **Vehicle <-> ground station link = raw 802.11 over a monitor-mode WiFi card
  (libpcap), or a serial link (SiK / ELRS).** There is no UDP socket in the
  flight path.

  Evidence:

  (608), `pcap_activate` (611), `pcap_setnonblock` (614).

  0x13123456 && ether[0x04:1] == 0x%.2x` — i.e. it matches the Ruby magic
  `0x13123456` in the 802.11 frame.

  (e.g. `PACKET_COMPONENT_COMMANDS`).

  **Verdict for §5:** the command path is implemented end-to-end. It is gated
  hard at the UI by telemetry-received, so on a radio-less desktop *no command
  is ever attempted* — the function returns false silently at
  `handle_commands.cpp:2331` (there is no user-visible error path there).

  ## 6. Precisely where a desktop with no radio breaks

  ## 7. Genuine defects found while reading (independent of the missing radio)

  1. **POSIX shm names missing the mandatory leading `/`.**
  `/mnt/Giochi-e-Altro-2/RubyFPV/RubyFPV/code/base/shared_mem.h:18-19`:
     `#define SHARED_MEM_RC_DOWNLOAD_INFO
  "R_SHARED_MEM_VEHICLE_RC_DOWNLOAD_INFO"` and
     `#define SHARED_MEM_RC_UPSTREAM_FRAME "R_SHARED_MEM_RC_UPSTREAM_FRAME"`,
     and `/mnt/Giochi-e-Altro-2/RubyFPV/RubyFPV/code/base/shared_mem_controller_
  only.h:5`
     `#define SHARED_MEM_CONTROLLER_ROUTER_VEHICLES_INFO
  "R_SHARED_MEM_CONTROLLER_ROUTER_VEHICLE_INFO"`.
     Every other shm name in the same headers has the leading `/` (e.g.
  `"/SYSTEM_SHARED_MEM_RUBY_RADIO_STATS"`, shared_mem.h:12). `shm_open` on Linux
  requires a leading `/`; without it the name is invalid and `open_shared_mem`
  (`shared_mem.c:40-67`) fails. The RC downstream/upstream channel and the
  router vehicles-info block are therefore the three shared-memory objects most
  likely to fail to open. **This is the kind of thing that would break the RC
  path even with a radio present.**
  2. **`ruby_close_ipc_channel` destroys the queue for both peers.**
  `/mnt/Giochi-e-Altro-2/RubyFPV/RubyFPV/code/base/ruby_ipc.c:449`, with
  `msgctl(fd, IPC_RMID, NULL)` at **:478**. Since both endpoints of a logical
  channel are separate `msgget()` handles on the same key, whoever closes first
  unlinks the queue for the other side.
  3. **`ruby_rx_telemetry` is not on the OSD path** — it is easy to mistake it
  for the telemetry consumer. The UI's telemetry comes from the router→central
  msgqueue; `ruby_rx_telemetry` only handles the datalink-download /
  raw-telemetry-download / RC-telemetry side channels.
  4. **IPC `msgsnd` is `IPC_NOWAIT` with only a 2×10 ms retry**
  (`ruby_ipc.c:580-655`), and the UI's router queue overflows by discarding
  *telemetry* messages (`r_central/process_router_messages.cpp:1893-1910`).
  Under load on desktop (no hardware pacing) this is where telemetry would
  silently be dropped.
  5. `r_station/packets_utils.cpp:756-763` and `r_vehicle/packets_utils.cpp`
  treat "no radio interface" as a soft skip with a 20 s log throttle — the
  failure is not surfaced to the UI as an alarm.

  ---

  ## 8. Bottom line

  - The desktop port is a **faithful, complete re-implementation of the flight
  path**, not a stub: joystick → RC packet → msgqueue → router → libpcap 802.11
  → vehicle router → msgqueue → RC decode → MAVLink `rc_channels_override` is
  all present with real code, and telemetry → msgqueue →
  `g_VehiclesRuntimeInfo[]` → Cairo/SDL2 OSD is all present with real code.
  - The **only** thing missing on a desktop with no radio is the radio itself.
  The chain breaks at `pairing.cpp:77-82` (nothing launches without a radio
  interface) and, if the router is force-started, at
  `r_station/packets_utils.cpp:756-763` (TX) and
  `r_central/handle_commands.cpp:2331` (all commands gated on received
  telemetry).
  - Two real bugs are independent of the missing hardware: the three `shm_open`
  names missing a leading `/` (shared_mem.h:18-19,
  shared_mem_controller_only.h:5) and `msgctl(IPC_RMID)` on channel close
  (ruby_ipc.c:478).

      642 +// Builds the list of the serial devices that could host a SiK
          + radio.                                                       
      643 +//                                                            
      644 +// On the embedded platforms the list is the fixed one, the US
          +B serial ports                                                
      645 +// of the board. On a generic Linux desktop the radio can be o
          +n any USB serial                                              
      646 +// device (a ttyUSB one or a CDC-ACM one) and it can be behind
          + a                                                            
      647 +// /dev/serial/by-id symlink, so the list is built from the en
          +umerated serial                                               
      648 +// ports and from the by-id symlinks. The devices that are alr
          +eady used for                                                 
      649 +// something else (a flight controller on the telemetry port, 
          +a core plugin)                                                
      650 +// are not probed, so that the AT commands are not sent to the
          +m.                                                            
      651 +//                                                            
      652 +// The environment variable RUBY_SIK_PORTS overrides the list,
          + it accepts a                                                 
      653 +// list of device paths separated by ':'. It is the way to poi
          +nt the                                                        
      654 +// application to a radio that is not detected by the enumerat

      655 +static int _hardware_radio_sik_get_candidate_devices(char szDe

      672 +                                                              
      673 +   #ifdef HW_PLATFORM_LINUX_GENERIC

      628 +// Stops a process, giving it the time to stop by itself.     
      629 +//                                                            
      630 +// The process is asked to stop with the SIGTERM signal, so th
          +at it can close                                               
      631 +// its resources (the user interface window, the shared memory
          +, the message                                                 
      632 +// queues), and it is killed only if it does not exit in the g
          +iven time.                                                    
      633 +// This is used for the processes that need more than the defa
          +ult grace time                                                
      634 +// to stop, ex: the user interface process.                   
      635 +void hw_stop_process_graceful(const char* szProcName, u32 uGra
          +ceMs)                                                         
      636 +{                                                             
      637 +   char szComm[1024];                                         
      638 +   char szPIDs[512];                                          
      639 +                                                              
      640 +   if ( NULL == szProcName || 0 == szProcName[0] )            
      641 +      return;                                                 
      642 +                                                              
      643 +   log_line("Stopping process [%s]...", szProcName);          
      644 +                                                              
      645 +   hw_process_get_pids(szProcName, szPIDs);                   
      646 +   removeTrailingNewLines(szPIDs);                            
      647 +   replaceNewLinesToSpaces(szPIDs);                           
      648 +   if ( strlen(szPIDs) <= 2 )                                 
      649 +   {                                                          
      650 +      log_line("Process [%s] does not exists.", szProcName);  
      651 +      return;                                                 
      652 +   }                                                          
      653 +                                                              
      654 +   log_line("Found PID(s) for process to stop %s: %s", szProcN
          +ame, szPIDs);                                                 
      655 +   sprintf(szComm, "kill %s 2>/dev/null", szPIDs);            
      656 +   hw_execute_bash_command(szComm, NULL);                     
      657 +                                                              
      658 +   u32 uTimeStart = get_current_timestamp_ms();               
      659 +   while ( get_current_timestamp_ms() < uTimeStart + uGraceMs 
          +)                                                             
      660 +   {                                                          
      661 +      hardware_sleep_ms(50);                                  
      662 +      szPIDs[0] = 0;                                          
      663 +      hw_process_get_pids(szProcName, szPIDs);                
      664 +      removeTrailingNewLines(szPIDs);                         
      665 +      replaceNewLinesToSpaces(szPIDs);                        
      666 +      if ( strlen(szPIDs) < 2 )                               
      667 +      {                                                       
      668 +         log_line("Did stopped process %s", szProcName);      
      669 +         return;                                              
      670 +      }                                                       
      671 +   }                                                          
      672 +                                                              
      673 +   log_softerror_and_alarm("The process %s did not stop in %u 
          +ms, killing it.", szProcName, uGraceMs);                      
      674 +   sprintf(szComm, "kill -9 %s 2>/dev/null", szPIDs);         
      675 +   hw_execute_bash_command(szComm, NULL);                     
      676 +   hardware_sleep_ms(20);                                     
      677 +}

● The port work is complete for this session and the three mission documents are
  written in the repository root.

  What I did this session

  SiK serial radio path (mission priority #2) — detection now walks a dynamic
  candidate list (RUBY_SIK_PORTS, enumerated serial ports, /dev/ttyACM*,
  /dev/serial/by-id/*), the open path no longer requires the device to be in the
  enumerated table, and a detected radio is registered and persisted to
  hw_serial.cfg. New in-repo regression test
  code/r_tests/test_sik_serial_path.cpp drives the production code end-to-end
  over a PTY (detect → open → write → real RX thread): 25 checks, 0 failures.

  Application lifecycle (priority #1) — hw_stop_process_graceful(); the
  controller now stops the UI gracefully (SIGTERM → "Finished shutdown UI" in ~1
  s, no SIGKILL); new ./ruby_start -stop leaves no Ruby process behind.

  Biggest find — the configuration was wiped on every start. The stale-FIFO
  cleanup used rm -rf /tmp/ruby/*, and on the desktop the config lives in
  /tmp/ruby/config/. I found it with an LD_PRELOAD shim logging every
  system/popen/unlink. The cleanup now removes only the named pipes, each by
  explicit name (RUBY_FIFO_NAMES). Settings now survive a restart.

  Honest error reporting — TX power no longer claims "changed to: 10" after an
  EPERM; unsupported radios are informational, not alarms; the absent
  ruby_rt_station is no longer an error when no radio exists (launcher and start
  script now share hardware_radio_has_serial_radios()); the base version file
  is found (11.8); first-run "missing file" messages now create the file.

  Final state: build clean, test_video_rx_pipeline 66/66,
  test_radio_capabilities 393/393, test_menu_rf_profiles 43/43,
  test_sik_serial_path 25/25, git diff --check clean. wlan0 stayed up on "Issam
  2.4g" (0% packet loss before and after), wlan1 untouched, regulatory domain
  unchanged, the 5 GHz-only guard intact, nothing run as root.

  Documents

  STATUS.md, QUESTIONS.md, PROGRESS.md in
  /mnt/Giochi-e-Altro-2/RubyFPV/RubyFPV/.

  Honest bottom line

  Live RF reception is still not validated, and the system is not flight-ready.
  rtw88_core.ko has no monitor-mode implementation at all, so the pcap RF path
  cannot work with the present USB card; the only monitor-capable driver here is
  on wlan0, which must not be touched. Two decisions are waiting for you in
  QUESTIONS.md: a monitor-mode-capable adapter (or approval for an out-of-tree 
  DKMS driver) and a 2.4+5.8 GHz adapter for the 2.4 GHz link. I also sent a
  desktop notification about this milestone.

❯ ## Decisions on QUESTIONS.md — 2026-10-22                                     
                                                                                
  ### Q1 — Monitor-mode radio adapter                                           
  **Decision: B, prepare for a separate compatible USB adapter. Do not          
  implement A yet.**                                                            
                                                                                
  Do not install a DKMS driver, modify the kernel, or reboot for this project   
  without asking me first. Research exact compatible chipsets and Linux         
  drivers, with evidence that they support the packet-capture behavior RubyFPV  
  actually needs. Do not assume a chipset name alone guarantees compatibility.  
                                                                                
  Option C is not a substitute for the 802.11 pcap path unless the project      
  explicitly supports that radio protocol as a complete alternative. Keep the   
  existing serial-radio implementation, but do not expand SiK support during    
  this phase.                                                                   
                                                                                
  Continue software-side port work while hardware is unavailable.               
                                                                                
  ### Q2 — 2.4 GHz versus 5.8 GHz                                               
  **Decision: use 5.8 GHz as the initial reference band for software            
  integration, but do not claim 2.4 GHz support has been validated.**           
                                                                                
  Do not weaken the antenna safety guard or tune the existing adapter to 2.4    
  GHz. Document the separate 2.4 GHz hardware requirement. Any eventual adapter 
  recommendation must explicitly support the required bands and RubyFPV's       
  packet-capture needs.                                                         
                                                                                
  ### Q3 — Persistent desktop configuration                                     
  **Decision: yes, move desktop user configuration to `~/.config/rubyfpv/`.**   
                                                                                
  Keep `/tmp/ruby/` for runtime-only data such as FIFOs, temporary media, and   
  logs. Preserve the embedded configuration layout. Inspect all `FOLDER_*`      
  definitions and their consumers before changing paths. Migrate existing       
  desktop settings safely where practical, without deleting or overwriting      
  configuration. Add a regression test demonstrating that configuration         
  survives application restarts and is stored persistently.                     
                                                                                
  ### Q4 — User-level systemd service                                           
  **Decision: defer automatic startup until the core port is stable.**          
                                                                                
  First make manual startup and shutdown reliable and document them. You may    
  investigate a user-level systemd unit, but do not enable it automatically,    
  install system-wide services, or create a service that starts the application 
  unexpectedly. If implemented, keep it optional and document how to enable,    
  start, stop, and disable it.                                                  
                                                                                
  ### Q5 — Vehicle-side scope                                                   
  **Decision: ground-station operation is the primary desktop target.**         
                                                                                
  Vehicle-side processes should compile and remain compatible, but do not       
  attempt to run them against nonexistent hardware or invent a desktop vehicle  
  simulation unless it is needed for a focused regression test. Prioritize the  
  ground station's real control-link integration, telemetry handling,           
  configuration, and video reception. Clearly document which functions require  
  embedded vehicle hardware.                                                    
                                                                                
  ### Q6 — Repeated EPERM messages                                              
  **Decision: improve the behavior if it can be done safely and accurately.**   
                                                                                
  Check whether the required capability is available before attempting          
  privileged radio configuration. If it is unavailable, skip the operation and  
  log a clear informational message. Do not silently claim success, hide        
  genuine failures, or change privileges to avoid the messages. Ensure the      
  radio remains correctly reported as unconfigured.                             
                                                                                
  ### Q7 — Old SiK fixture process                                              
  **Decision: stop it if you can verify that PID 129064 is still the exact      
  fixture described and not a reused PID.**                                     
                                                                                
  Verify the process command line and identity first. If it is still the        
  obsolete fixture, terminate only that process gracefully. Do not kill         
  unrelated Python processes or broadly clean temporary files.                  
                                                                                
  ### Next priorities                                                           
                                                                                
  After resolving the safe decisions above:                                     
                                                                                
  1. Implement and test persistent desktop configuration.                       
  2. Verify the complete startup/shutdown lifecycle and configuration           
  persistence.                                                                  
  3. Audit the remaining flight-critical ground-station functionality and fix   
  concrete software defects.                                                    
  4. Research compatible RF hardware without installing drivers or changing     
  network settings.                                                             
  5. Re-run the relevant build and regression suites.                           
  6. Update `STATUS.md`, `QUESTIONS.md`, and `PROGRESS.md` with evidence and    
  remaining hardware-dependent blockers.                                        
                                                                                
  Continue autonomously. Preserve the existing worktree and passing tests. Do   
  not claim flight readiness without real hardware validation.                    ⎿  2 skills available

      1568 +int hw_process_has_net_admin_capability()                    
      1569 +{                                                            
      1570 +   // Configuring a wireless interface (mode, channel, freque
           +ncy, power) needs                                            
      1571 +   // the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability. The effective capabilitie
           +s of the process                                             
      1572 +   // are read from the proc filesystem, so that no library i
           +s needed and no                                              
      1573 +   // privilege is changed in any way.                       
      1574 +   #define CAP_NET_ADMIN_BIT 12                              
      1575 +                                                             
      1576 +   FILE* fd = fopen("/proc/self/status", "r");               
      1577 +   if ( NULL == fd )                                         
      1578 +      return 0;                                              
      1579 +                                                             
      1580 +   char szLine[256];                                         
      1581 +   bool bFound = false;                                      
      1582 +   unsigned long long uEffective = 0;                        
      1583 +   while ( NULL != fgets(szLine, sizeof(szLine), fd) )       
      1584 +   {                                                         
      1585 +      if ( 0 != strncmp(szLine, "CapEff:", 7) )              
      1586 +         continue;                                           
      1587 +      uEffective = strtoull(&szLine[7], NULL, 16);           
      1588 +      bFound = true;                                         
      1589 +      break;                                                 
      1590 +   }                                                         
      1591 +   fclose(fd);                                               
      1592 +                                                             
      1593 +   if ( ! bFound )                                           
      1594 +      return 0;                                              
      1595 +                                                             
      1596 +   return ( 0 != ( (uEffective >> CAP_NET_ADMIN_BIT) & 1 ) ) 
           +? 1 : 0;                                                     
      1597 +}                                                            
      1598 +

❯ # RubyFPV Desktop Port — Video Streaming First, Two-Radio RF Loopback         
                                                                                
  ## Primary objective                                                          
                                                                                
  **Make end-to-end video streaming work. This is the highest priority.**       
                                                                                
  We need RubyFPV to receive live video through its real VRX/RF reception path, 
  reconstruct and display it in the Linux desktop ground station, and           
  correctly implement any required video forwarding/retransmission toward the   
  VTX according to the existing architecture.                                   
                                                                                
  Do not spend time on SiK support, unrelated features, cosmetic UI work, or    
  optional integrations while video streaming remains blocked.                  
                                                                                
  ## 1. Fixed hardware assignment                                               
                                                                                
  I already own two working USB Wi-Fi adapters:                                 
                                                                                
  - **TX / emulated VTX: TP-Link Archer T2U Plus.**                             
  - **RX / VRX: Eachine WiFiLink USB adapter**, which I have tested with        
  OpenIPC.                                                                      
  - **`wlan0`: active network connection. Leave it completely untouched.**      
                                                                                
  Use the TP-Link as the dedicated transmitting adapter and the Eachine as the  
  dedicated receiving adapter. Do not swap these assignments without asking.    
                                                                                
  First identify both adapters using USB hardware IDs, chipset, interface name, 
  and loaded driver. Do not rely on interface names alone because they may      
  change between boots.                                                         
                                                                                
  The fact that the Eachine works with OpenIPC is useful evidence, but it does  
  not by itself prove compatibility with RubyFPV's RF protocol.                 
                                                                                
  ## 2. Trace the actual production video path                                  
                                                                                
  Before making broad changes, map the real code path end to end:               
                                                                                
  1. Video source and encoding.                                                 
  2. VTX-side packet framing and transmission.                                  
  3. RF reception through the VRX adapter.                                      
  4. Packet parsing, reassembly, and video reconstruction.                      
  5. FIFO/socket or other IPC boundaries.                                       
  6. Desktop player startup and live playback.                                  
  7. Required forwarding/retransmission toward the VTX, if applicable to the    
  existing protocol.                                                            
  8. Stream interruption, recovery, and shutdown.                               
                                                                                
  Identify the concrete production functions, files, threads, protocols, packet 
  formats, and hardware dependencies involved. Compare the desktop              
  implementation with the existing embedded implementation wherever that helps  
  establish correct behavior.                                                   
                                                                                
  Do not invent a protocol or assume retransmission means a particular thing.   
  Trace the existing architecture first.                                        
                                                                                
  ## 3. Implement the two-radio test                                            
                                                                                
  Build a repeatable test using the fixed adapter assignments:                  
                                                                                
  - TP-Link Archer T2U Plus transmits protocol-valid VTX-side traffic.          
  - Eachine WiFiLink receives it through RubyFPV's real VRX reception path.     
  - Received packets pass through production parsing, reconstruction, and       
  desktop playback.                                                             
  - Any required VTX forwarding/retransmission path is tested independently.    
                                                                                
  First inspect the actual Linux driver capabilities of both adapters,          
  including monitor mode, packet injection/transmission requirements, supported 
  bands/channels, and the RF mode RubyFPV actually uses.                        
                                                                                
  Use 5.8 GHz as the initial test target if both adapters and the relevant      
  hardware configuration support it. Check channel compatibility and receiver   
  desensitization; do not assume two adapters can reliably communicate merely   
  because both work with ordinary Wi-Fi.                                        
                                                                                
  Determine whether OpenIPC can provide a compatible transmitter or whether a   
  protocol-valid emulator is required. Ordinary Wi-Fi traffic, successful       
  packet injection, or a generated video file is not sufficient proof that      
  RubyFPV's RF protocol works.                                                  
                                                                                
  If either adapter cannot support the required path, document the precise

  ## 1. CRASH — `_hw_execute_bash_command()` writes up to ~4 KB into caller
  buffers of 256/512 bytes (stack overflow)

  **File / lines:** `code/base/hardware_procs.cpp:1205-1246` (helper), callers
  `code/base/hardware_procs.cpp:592` (`hw_stop_process`), `:644`
  (`hw_stop_process_graceful`), `:689` (`hw_kill_process`).

  ```c
  // hardware_procs.cpp:1217-1238
     char szBuff[2048];
     ...
        iRead = fread(szBuff, 1, 1022, fp);
        if ( iRead > 0 )
        {
           iCountRead += iRead;
           if ( (NULL != pOut) && (iCountRead < 4094) )
           {
              szBuff[iRead] = 0;
              memcpy(pOut, szBuff, iRead+1);
              pOut += iRead;
           }
        }
  ```
  ```c
  // hardware_procs.cpp:591-600
  void hw_stop_process(const char* szProcName)
  {
     char szComm[1024];
     char szPIDs[512];
     ...
     hw_process_get_pids(szProcName, szPIDs);
  ```
  The helper has **no output-size parameter**: the only limit is the hard-coded
  4094 bytes. Every caller of `hw_execute_bash_command*()` therefore gets up to
  4093 bytes written into a buffer of whatever size it declared (`szPIDs[512]`
  in `hw_stop_process`/`hw_stop_process_graceful`, `szPIDs[256]` in
  `hw_kill_process`, `szOutput[1024]` at `hardware_procs.cpp:228,306`).

  **Failure scenario:** the PID lookup falls back to `ps -ae | grep <name> |
  grep -v "grep"` (`hardware_procs.cpp:526`) whenever `pidof` and `pgrep` fail.
  `ps -ae` prints the *full command line* of every process, each line being
  100-150 bytes. As soon as 4-5 command lines contain the process name, the
  output exceeds 512 bytes and the `memcpy` overwrites the stack of
  `hw_stop_process` past `szPIDs[512]`, smashing the return address of the
  process that is shutting the station down (`ruby_start -stop` →
  `_stop_all_processes()` → `hw_stop_process_graceful`).

  **Confidence: high.** The size mismatch is unconditional in the code (no size
  argument exists); only the *amount* of data needed to trigger it depends on
  the machine's process list.

  ## 2. CRASH — `hw_process_get_pids()` `ps` fallback matches unrelated
  processes, which are then `kill -9`-ed

  **File / lines:** `code/base/hardware_procs.cpp:509-531` (lookup), `:626-641`
  and `:663-681` (the `kill` / `kill -9`).

  ```c
  // hardware_procs.cpp:515-518  (pgrep branch - the name IS escaped)
        if ( strlen(szProcName) > 15 )
           sprintf(szComm, "pgrep -f \"[/]%s\" 2>/dev/null", szProcName);
        else
           sprintf(szComm, "pgrep %s 2>/dev/null", szProcName);
  ...
  // hardware_procs.cpp:526  (ps branch - the name is NOT escaped and matches
  the whole cmdline)
           sprintf(szComm, "ps -ae | grep %s | grep -v \"grep\"", szProcName);
  ```
  The `[/]` trick that prevents the search command from matching itself is
  applied **only** to the `pgrep` branch. The `ps` branch greps the whole
  command line of every process.

  **Failure scenario:** the user has any process whose command line merely
  *contains* the name — e.g. an editor with `ruby_central.cpp` open, a shell
  running `ruby_central --help`, a wrapper script
  `/usr/local/bin/ruby_logger_watch`, or a `tail -f` of a log whose path
  contains `ruby_video_proc`. `pidof` and `pgrep` (exact name) both fail, the
  `ps` branch matches those unrelated processes, and their PIDs are then passed
  to `kill -9` by `hw_stop_process`/`hw_stop_process_graceful`
  (`hardware_procs.cpp:626`, `:678`) — the station kills the user's unrelated
  programs. This runs on every shutdown of the ground station
  (`ruby_start.cpp:688-698`).

  **Confidence: high** that the code path behaves as described; the
  *probability* of the trigger depends on the user's process list, but the
  missing escape/scoping is a real difference from the sibling `pgrep` branch.

  outside `szName`.

  **Confidence: high** — the index `-1` is unconditional once the name is empty;
  the only question is how the file gets truncated, and finding 9 shows the

     strcat(szFile, FILE_CONFIG_UI_PREFERENCES);
     FILE* fd = fopen(szFile, "w");        // truncates the existing file first
  ```
  There is no temp-file + `rename()` anywhere in the settings writers. (The new
  migration code *does* implement the atomic pattern — `config_paths.c:184-223
  _config_copy_file()` — but only for the migration copy, not for the settings
  themselves.)

  **Failure scenario:** the ground station is killed (SIGKILL, power loss, OOM)
  in the middle of `save_Preferences()` / `save_ControllerSettings()` /
  `save_PluginsSettings()` / `save_CorePluginsSettings()` → the file is left
  truncated → on the next start the loader fails the stamp check or the field
  reads → `reset_Preferences()` / `reset_PluginsSettings()` /
  `reset_CorePluginsSettings()` is called and the file is **overwritten with the
  defaults**: the user's OSD layout, quick-button actions, controller settings,
  plugin positions and plugin enable flags are silently and permanently lost.
  For `rf_profiles.cfg` the file has a size header and a CRC32
  (`radio_profiles.cpp:287-360`), so a truncated file is rejected outright and
  *all* RF profiles are lost with no way to recover them.

  **Confidence: high** — the write pattern is `fopen(...,"w")` followed by
  several `fprintf` calls; the crash window is the whole duration of the write.

  ---

  ## 10. PROCESS LIFECYCLE — the shutdown path never stops the update worker,
  which keeps overwriting the running installation

  **Files / lines:** `code/r_start/ruby_start.cpp:686-700` (stop path),
  `code/r_central/menu/menu_controller_update.cpp:254-262` (launch),
  `code/r_utils/ruby_update_worker.cpp:346-352` (what the worker does).

  ```c
  // ruby_start.cpp:688-698
     hw_stop_process_graceful("ruby_central", 5000);
     hw_stop_process_graceful("ruby_controller", 5000);
     hw_stop_process_graceful("ruby_rt_station", 3000);
     hw_stop_process_graceful("ruby_rt_router", 3000);
     hw_stop_process_graceful("ruby_tx_rc", 3000);
     hw_stop_process_graceful("ruby_rx_telemetry", 3000);
     hw_stop_process_graceful("ruby_video_proc", 3000);
     hw_stop_process_graceful("ruby_logger", 3000);
     //  no ruby_update_worker, no unzip
  ```
  ```c
  // menu_controller_update.cpp:261
        hw_execute_ruby_process(NULL, "ruby_update_worker", szUpdateFile, NULL);
  ```
  ```c
  // ruby_update_worker.cpp:348
     snprintf(szComm, ..., "cp -rf %sruby_* %s 2>/dev/null",
  szSrcBinariesFolder, FOLDER_BINARIES);
  ```
  A repository-wide grep shows that `ruby_update_worker` is referenced **only**
  in `menu_controller_update.cpp` (where it is *waited for*, never stopped) — no
  other ground-station file kills it.

  **Failure scenario:** the user starts "Update controller" from the menu and
  closes the RubyFPV window (or `ruby_start -stop` is invoked, or `ruby_central`
  crashes) while the update is in progress. The `ruby_update_worker` (and the
  `unzip` child it spawns) survives and keeps overwriting `/tmp/ruby/bin/ruby_*`
  and `/tmp/ruby/bin/res/*` with the new version. The watchdog
  (`ruby_controller`) then restarts `ruby_central`, which now starts from a
  **half-replaced binary set** → crash loop, or a station that runs a mix of two
  versions. The comment above `_stop_all_processes()` claims the stop "releases
  the resources (the window, the shared memory and the message queues)", which
  is not true for this child.

  **Confidence: high** — the process is launched by the central and is absent
  from every stop list in the project.

  ---

  ## 11. RADIO — on the desktop, opening a radio link silently reconfigures the
  interface (monitor mode + frequency + bandwidth + TX power) from a stored
  profile

  **Files / lines:** `code/r_station/radio_links.cpp:1000-1015` (the automatic
  application), `code/base/radio_profiles.cpp:485-510` (interface resolution),
  `:771-914` (what is applied).

  ```c
  // radio_links.cpp:1006-1015  (inside the radio-link opening path, no platform
  guard)
        {
           char szProfileError[512];
           szProfileError[0] = 0;
           int iProfileApplied = radio_profiles_apply_to_interface(i,
  szProfileError, sizeof(szProfileError)/sizeof(szProfileError[0]));
  ```
  ```c
  // radio_profiles.cpp:490-508
     if ( pProfile->iInterfaceIndex != RADIO_PROFILE_IFACE_AUTO )
     {
        if ( (pProfile->iInterfaceIndex < 0) || (pProfile->iInterfaceIndex >=
  hardware_get_radio_interfaces_count()) )
           return -1;
        return pProfile->iInterfaceIndex;          // bound by ENUMERATION INDEX
     }
     // pick the first usable WiFi radio interface
     for( int i=0; i<hardware_get_radio_interfaces_count(); i++ )
     { ... return i; }                             // AUTO = the FIRST WiFi
  adapter
  ```
  `radio_profiles_configure_interface()` then calls
  `radio_cap_set_monitor_mode(i, 1)`,
  `radio_utils_set_interface_frequency_and_bandwidth(i, freq, htFlag)` and the
  raw TX-power setters (`radio_profiles.cpp:846-911`). The whole path is **not**
  guarded by `HW_PLATFORM_LINUX_GENERIC` and does **not** check
  `hw_process_has_net_admin_capability()` — unlike the rest of the desktop radio
  code, which is explicitly guarded (`radio_links.cpp:75-88, 97-131, 159-184,
  1569-1613`) and unlike `code/r_start/r_initradio.cpp:166`, which does check
  the capability before touching a radio.

  **Failure scenario:** the profile binds to an adapter by *enumeration index*,
  or `AUTO` = "the first usable WiFi radio interface". On a desktop the first
  WiFi adapter is frequently the **built-in** one (the one carrying the user's
  internet connection), not the USB RubyFPV radio. The profile file is also
  copied verbatim by the new migration (`config_paths.c:286`,
  `config_copy_settings_folder("/tmp/ruby/config/", "~/.config/rubyfpv/")`), so
  a profile written for a different adapter layout is silently adopted. Result:
  when the user connects to a vehicle, the station puts the *internal* adapter
  into monitor mode and retunes it to the link frequency — the machine loses its
  network connection, without any user action, without any confirmation dialog
  and without any privilege check. The user has no way to know which adapter was
  touched, since the binding is an index, not a MAC/name.

  **Confidence: medium-high** that this is the defect the audit brief describes
  ("the radio interfaces must NEVER be reconfigured automatically on the
  desktop"). Counter-argument to note: putting the *dedicated* RubyFPV adapter
  in monitor mode at link-open is by design (the desktop build has no other way
  to talk to the vehicle), and the applied frequency is validated against the
  regulatory domain by `radio_cap_validate_request()` before it is written to
  the card. The defect is that (a) the frequency/bandwidth/TX-power part is
  applied silently from a config file with no user action, and (b) the adapter
  to which it is applied is selected by index/AUTO, so the *wrong* adapter (the
  internal WiFi) can be reconfigured.

  ---

  ## 12. SETTING LOST — a failed read resets the wrong preference

  **File / lines:** `code/base/ctrl_preferences.c:343-353`.

  ```c
  343   if ( bOk && 1 != fscanf(fd, "%d", &s_Preferences.iDebugShowFullRXStats)
  )
  344   {
  345      s_Preferences.iDebugShowFullRXStats = 0;
  346      bOk = 0;
  347   }
  348
  349   if ( bOk && 1 != fscanf(fd, "%d", &s_Preferences.iDebugWiFiChangeDelay)
  )
  350   {
  351      s_Preferences.iDebugShowFullRXStats = 0;   // <-- wrong variable
  352      bOk = 0;
  353   }
  ```
  **Failure scenario:** the preferences file ends right after the
  `iDebugShowFullRXStats` line (a truncated file, see finding 9). The read of
  `iDebugShowFullRXStats` at line 343 succeeded, but the failure of the *next*
  field resets `iDebugShowFullRXStats` to 0 — the user's "show full RX stats"
  setting is silently lost, and `iDebugWiFiChangeDelay` keeps whatever stale
  value it had. The line clearly intends `s_Preferences.iDebugWiFiChangeDelay =
  0;`.

  **Confidence: high** — a copy/paste error, and it produces exactly the "a
  setting is silently lost" symptom the brief asks about.

  ## Areas checked where I found no concrete defect

  * **Radio frequency/regulatory changes from the UI menus** —
  `code/r_central/menu/menu_radio_config.cpp` validates every link/interface
  index against `links_count` before touching
  `radioLinksParams`/`radioInterfacesParams` (`:748, 766, 834, 858`); the radio
  menus do not call the frequency setter directly (only `menu_rf_profiles.cpp` →
  `radio_profiles_apply()`, which validates the request against the regulatory
  domain first).
  * **The other desktop radio operations** (network service restart, udev
  restart, interface cycling, monitor-mode setup) are correctly guarded with
  `HW_PLATFORM_LINUX_GENERIC` (`radio_links.cpp:75-88, 97-131, 159-184,
  1569-1613`).
  * **`sudo` usage in `ruby_start.cpp`** — all `system("sudo mount ...")` calls
  (`:479, 922-932, 1019-1032, 2034`) are inside the Raspberry/Radxa-specific
  code paths, not the desktop build.
  * **Process shutdown ordering in `code/r_central/launchers_controller.cpp`** —
  the desktop guards (serial radio, i2c, tx_rc) are present and the wait list
  matches the launched processes.
  * **Vehicle-side code** — not audited, as requested.

  Minor/latent items noted but not promoted to findings (no concrete trigger
  found): `getSpectatorModel()` (`models_list.cpp:254`) uses `iIndex >
  s_iModelsSpectatorCount` instead of `>=` (off-by-one, but all current callers
  pass an index strictly below the count and check for NULL);
  `config_get_vehicle_history_folder()` (`config_paths.c:162-168`) returns a
  shared static buffer (non-reentrant); `config_copy_settings_folder()` uses
  `strncat` with a total-size argument (`config_paths.c:243, 246`) — harmless
  here because of the preceding empty-string guard.

  RubyFPV ground-station control-link / telemetry audit (desktop x86_64 build,
  RUBY_BUILD_ENV=desktop -> HW_PLATFORM_LINUX_GENERIC). Read-only; nothing was

  All paths are absolute. Severity order: crash / memory corruption first, then
  loss of control or wrong control-relevant state, then hardening gaps.

  =====================================================================
  F1  [CRASH - heap buffer overflow] Missing length check before the RX-queue
  memcpy
  =====================================================================
  (1) Files / lines
  /mnt/Giochi-e-Altro-2/RubyFPV/RubyFPV/code/radio/radio_rx.c:451-477
  (producer), :302 (consumer), :1257 & :1271 (buffer allocation), :604-613
  (serial source), :843 (wifi source)
  /mnt/Giochi-e-Altro-2/RubyFPV/RubyFPV/code/radio/radiolink.c:1311-1323 (wifi
  length validation)

  (2) Code
  ```c
  // radio_rx.c
  451 void _radio_rx_add_packet_to_rx_queue(u8* pPacket, int iLength, int
  iRadioInterface)
  ...
  476    pQueue->iPacketsLengths[iIndexToWriteTo] = iLength;
  477    memcpy(pQueue->pPacketsBuffers[iIndexToWriteTo], pPacket, iLength);
  // no check on iLength
  ...
  1257:  s_RadioRxState.queue_reg_priority.pPacketsBuffers[i] = (u8*)
  malloc(MAX_PACKET_TOTAL_SIZE);  // 1500 bytes
  // consumer, proves the intended invariant (but the producer never enforces
  it):
  302:  ... && (pQueue->iPacketsLengths[iIndexToCopy] > 0) &&
  (pQueue->iPacketsLengths[iIndexToCopy] < MAX_PACKET_TOTAL_SIZE)
  // wifi path
  843:  _radio_rx_check_add_packet_to_rx_queue(pPacketBuffer, iPacketLength,
  iInterfaceIndex);
  // radiolink.c
  1311  int iPacketLength = pPH->total_length;
  1314  if ( iPacketLength > iBufferLength ) { ... return 0; }   // only "fits
  in the captured frame" - never compared with MAX_PACKET_TOTAL_SIZE
  ```
  (3) Failure scenario
  The packet length used for the copy is `pPH->total_length` (u16,
  peer-controlled) and the only validation is "does it fit in the captured
  802.11 frame" (radiolink.c:1314). A peer on the radio link (a
  compromised/rogue vehicle, or anyone able to inject an 802.11 frame on the
  video/data radio) sends a radiotap+802.11 frame whose payload is e.g. 2000
  bytes and whose Ruby header claims `total_length = 2000`, with a correct CRC32
  (the CRC convention is `crc32(buf+4, total_length-4)` stored in bytes 0..3,
  so the attacker can compute it). The frame passes `packet_process_and_check`
  (CRC ok), and radio_rx.c:843 -> :477 memcpy's 2000 bytes into a 1500-byte
  `malloc()` buffer: a 500-byte heap overflow in ruby_rt_station, with
  attacker-controlled content.
  The same overflow is reachable without pcap: the serial (SiK) short-packet
  reassembly path accumulates up to 3000 bytes (radio_rx.c:550
  `s_uBuffersFullMessages[MAX_RADIO_INTERFACES][MAX_PACKET_TOTAL_SIZE*2]`) and
  at radio_rx.c:604-613 accepts any `pPH->total_length` that fits in the
  reassembled buffer, i.e. up to 3000, and hands it to the same memcpy -> up to
  1500 bytes of heap overflow.
  Observable effect: heap corruption / SIGSEGV in the router process; with luck,
  adjacent heap objects (the other queue entries, the shared-memory structs)
  are corrupted. The consumer's own `iPacketsLengths < MAX_PACKET_TOTAL_SIZE`
  test (line 302) means the oversized packet is later discarded, but the damage
  is already done at enqueue time.
  (4) Confidence: HIGH. Producer/consumer asymmetry on the same queue, the
  buffer size is a hard 1500 (`MAX_PACKET_TOTAL_SIZE`, radiopackets2.h:54) and
  the producer memcpy has no bound at all. Both source paths (wifi and serial)
  accept a peer-chosen `total_length` larger than 1500. Only the fact that a
  legitimate RubyFPV vehicle never builds a >1500-byte packet keeps this from
  firing by accident - the receiving side has no such guarantee.

  F5  [CRASH - static buffer overflow] pcap payload length taken from the wire
  length, not the captured length
  =====================================================================
  (1) File / lines
  /mnt/Giochi-e-Altro-2/RubyFPV/RubyFPV/code/radio/radiolink.c:1061-1066 and
  :1276
  buffer: /mnt/Giochi-e-Altro-2/RubyFPV/RubyFPV/code/radio/radiolink.c:64 with
  /mnt/Giochi-e-Altro-2/RubyFPV/RubyFPV/code/radio/radiolink.h:43
  snaplen: /mnt/Giochi-e-Altro-2/RubyFPV/RubyFPV/code/radio/radiolink.c:618-620

  (2) Code
  ```c
  64     u8 sPayloadBufferRead[MAX_PACKET_LENGTH_PCAP];        // radiolink.h:43
  -> 4096 bytes
  ...
  618    int iLen = MAX_PACKET_TOTAL_SIZE*6;                    // pcap snaplen
  = 9000
  ...
  1061   sRadioLastReceivedHeadersLength = rti.max_length +
  sizeof(s_uIEEEHeaderData);
  1063   payloadLength = ppcapPacketHeader->len -
  sRadioLastReceivedHeadersLength;   // 'len' = on-the-wire length, not 'caplen'
  1066   payloadLength -= 4;                                    // (FCS)
  ...
  1276   memcpy(sPayloadBufferRead, pRadioPayload, payloadLength);   // no bound
  check, dst is 4096 bytes
  ```
  (3) Failure scenario
  `pcap_pkthdr.len` is the original frame length; only `caplen` bytes are
  actually available in libpcap's buffer. The code derives the copy length from
  `len` and copies into the 4096-byte static buffer without any clamp. A frame
  that is longer than 4096 bytes (802.11 A-MSDU/A-MPDU aggregated frames reach
  8-11 KB; the configured snaplen is 9000, so such frames are captured) makes
  `payloadLength` ~4000-9000 -> a 4-5 KB overflow of `sPayloadBufferRead` and a
  read past the end of libpcap's packet buffer. If `len` is smaller than the
  parsed header length, `payloadLength` becomes negative and is passed to
  `memcpy` as a huge `size_t` -> immediate crash.
  The same code path is reachable deterministically with the pcap-file replay
  feature (`radio_open_interface_for_read_from_file`, radiolink.c:723, used by
  code/r_tests/test_video_rx_pipeline.cpp): a crafted capture file whose packet
  header declares `len = 60000` overflows deterministically.
  Observable effect: crash of the router (SIGSEGV) or corruption of adjacent
  .bss globals.
  (4) Confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH. The missing bound check on the memcpy is certain;
  the practical trigger requires a frame larger than 4096 bytes to reach the GS
  radio interface (or the pcap replay path, which is deterministic). The `len`
  vs `caplen` confusion is a genuine bug that pcap's own documentation warns
  about.

  F6  [WRONG CONTROL-RELEVANT TELEMETRY] LTM S-frame: ARMED and flight mode are

  (1) File / lines
  /mnt/Giochi-e-Altro-2/RubyFPV/RubyFPV/code/base/parse_fc_telemetry_ltm.cpp:198
  -275 (S-frame handler), :51 (frame length), :85-103 (byte readers)

  (2) Code
  ```c
  198    if ( s_LTMExpectedFrameType == LIGHTTELEMETRY_SFRAME )
  199    {
  201       //Vbat uint16, mV / Battery Consumption uint16, mAh / RSSI uchar /
  Airspeed uchar / Status uchar
  207       pdpfct->voltage = parse_ltm_read_u16();
  208       pdpfct->mah = parse_ltm_read_u16();
  209       pdpfct->rc_rssi = parse_ltm_read_u8();

  234       tmp8 = parse_ltm_read_u8();          // <-- payload byte index 5 =
  AIR SPEED, not the status byte (index 6)
  237       switch (( tmp8 >> 2) & 0b00111111 ) { ... pdpfct->flight_mode =
  FLIGHT_MODE_...; }
  263       if ( tmp8 & 0b00000001 )
  265          pdpfct->flight_mode |= FLIGHT_MODE_ARMED;
  266          pdpfct->uFCFlags |= FC_TELE_FLAGS_ARMED;
  ```
  LTM S-frame payload layout (7 bytes + checksum): vbat(2) mah(2) rssi(1)
  airspeed(1) status(1). The parser reads 4 of the 7 payload bytes; the 5th read
  lands on airspeed, and the real status byte (payload index 6) is never read.
  The frame length is right (`LIGHTTELEMETRY_SFRAMELENGTH 11` = '$','T','S' + 7
  payload + checksum, code/base/parse_fc_telemetry_ltm.cpp:51), so the status
  byte is present in the buffer - it is simply skipped.

  A vehicle flying at, say, 12 m/s sends airspeed = 12 (0b00001100). The ground
  station decodes status = 12 -> flight_mode = (12>>2)&0x3F = 3 =
  FLIGHT_MODE_HORZ (instead of the real mode) and ARMED = (12 & 1) = 0 -> the
  OSD shows "disarmed" while the vehicle is armed. With airspeed = 11 (0b01011)
  the GS shows "ARMED" and flight_mode = 2 = ACRO. Every displayed arm state and
  flight mode coming from an LTM (MAVLink-over-LTM) vehicle is wrong, and it
  changes with the airspeed.
  Observable effect: the operator sees a wrong arm state / wrong flight mode;
  the ground station's "vehicle armed" indication cannot be trusted (relevant
  when deciding to disarm or to take over).
  (4) Confidence: HIGH. The field order is fixed by the LTM protocol and is also
  written down in the comment block right above the code (lines 201-205) - the
  code simply reads one byte too early. The `status` byte is the last payload
  byte and is never consumed.

  ENABLING FACT that makes findings 1-4 concretely triggerable (not
  theoretical):
  Video packets are transmitted with HEADER-ONLY CRC: the vehicle sets
  PACKET_FLAGS_BIT_HEADERS_ONLY_CRC on every video packet
  (code/r_vehicle/video_tx_buffers.cpp:451 and :805), and the RX side honours it
  at code/radio/radiolink.c:1390-1393 (CRC computed over
  sizeof(t_packet_header) = 24 bytes only). The video segment header
  (t_packet_header_video_segment, 40 bytes: uCurrentBlockIndex,
  uCurrentBlockPacketIndex, uCurrentBlockDataPackets, uCurrentBlockECPackets,
  uCurrentBlockPacketSize, radiopackets2.h:304-356) and the important header
  (uVideoDataLength, radiopackets2.h:358-364) therefore lie OUTSIDE the
  CRC-protected region. On the pcap/WiFi link the 802.11 FCS is not verified at
  all - radiolink.c:1118-1120 only strips the 4 FCS bytes from the length
  ("Ralink and Atheros both always supply the FCS to userspace") and never
  checks it. So on a marginal WiFi link a single bit error inside the video
  segment header is accepted by the station and the corrupted fields are used as
  ARRAY INDICES and LENGTHS with no bound check. (On the serial-radio path
  radio_rx.c:609 does compute a full-packet CRC, so there the trigger requires a
  CRC-valid malformed packet / a peer using a different block scheme; the
  station explicitly supports the vehicle changing the block scheme at runtime -
  "scheme changed" check at video_rx_buffers.cpp:376-385 - so an out-of-range
  scheme from a different vehicle build is also a live trigger.) I verified
  there is NO bound check on any of these fields anywhere in the RX path (grep
  of uCurrentBlockPacketIndex / uVideoDataLength over code/r_station and
  code/radio).

  Confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH (same trigger as finding 9; the destination is sized
  MAX_PACKET_TOTAL_SIZE while the source length is the unvalidated wire length).

  =====================================================================
  FINDING 11 - OOB READ: hasVideoPacket() indexes packets[] with an unbounded
  wire index
  File: code/r_station/video_rx_buffers.cpp line 462 (declared 448), called from
  code/r_station/processor_rx_video.cpp:506
    462: if ( m_VideoBlocks[iBufferIndex].packets[uVideoBlockPacketIndex].bEmpty
  )
  uVideoBlockPacketIndex is u32 and is passed as pPHVS->uCurrentBlockPacketIndex
  (u8, up to 255) with no range check against MAX_TOTAL_PACKETS_IN_BLOCK (32).
  Failure scenario: a packet with a corrupted packet index makes the station
  read a byte far outside the block struct (and the same corrupted value is then
  used by finding 1). Observable: wrong "already received" decisions (duplicate
  suppression broken -> blocks never complete -> video stalls) and an OOB read
  of the block array.
  Confidence: HIGH that the check is missing; the practical impact is smaller
  than finding 1 (read-only, 1 byte).

  =====================================================================
  FINDING 12 - DATA LOSS on the default (FIFO) output path: frame silently
  dropped when the staging buffer is full, and partial-write data loss
  File: code/r_station/rx_video_output.cpp lines 1003-1027
   1012: if ( iLength + s_iPipeVideoOutputPos < 250000 )
   1014:    memcpy(&(s_pPipeVideoOutputBuffer[s_iPipeVideoOutputPos]), pBuffer,
  iLength);
   1015:    s_iPipeVideoOutputPos += iLength;
   1017: if ( (! bWaitFullFrame) || (bWaitFullFrame && bIsEndOfNALFrame) )
   1021:    iRes = write(s_fPipeVideoOutToStreamer, s_pPipeVideoOutputBuffer,
  s_iPipeVideoOutputPos);
   1023:    s_iPipeVideoOutputPos = 0;
   1027: if ( iRes == iExpectedWriteResult ) { ... return; }   // "success" path
  There is no else branch at 1012: when the 250000-byte staging buffer cannot
  take the new frame, the frame is dropped with NO error, and the function still
  takes the success path (iRes == iExpectedWriteResult) so no alarm is raised
  and no error is counted. Additionally, s_iPipeVideoOutputPos is reset to 0 at
  1023 regardless of how many bytes the write() actually transferred, so a short
  write discards the unwritten remainder of the frame.
  Also note that this write() is a blocking write on the FIFO performed inline
  in the radio packet processing thread of ruby_rt_station
  (ruby_rt_station.cpp:750 -> ... -> rx_video_output_video_data). If the player
  stops draining the FIFO (GStreamer stall), the write blocks and the whole
  radio/telemetry processing of the station stalls; the only mitigation is the
  g_pProcessStats->uInBlockingOperation flag (1005/1007) which merely displays
  the condition in the UI.
  Confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH for the silent drop and the unconditional position
  reset (both are plainly visible); the blocking-write stall is a known/flagged
  design issue, so I rank it low.

  =====================================================================
  AREAS WITH NO CONCRETE DEFECT FOUND (checked, nothing to report):
  - code/r_station/packets_utils.cpp, code/r_station/radio_links.cpp,
  code/r_station/rx_video_recording_data.cpp, code/r_station/ruby_controller.cpp
  (watchdog): no video-path defect (the semaphores are opened O_CREAT and
  unlinked at exit only).
  - code/radio/fec.c: the VLA matrix[nr_fec_blocks*nr_fec_blocks] (fec.c:887)
  and the assert(nrDataBlocks<=128) (fec.c:820) are only unsafe through the
  upstream unchecked counts of finding 2, not on their own; with valid counts
  (<=16 data, <=16 EC) the FEC path is correct.
  - code/r_station/process_radio_in_packets.cpp: the video dispatch (line 1414)
  just forwards the packet/length; the length handling issue is upstream in
  finding 9/10.
  Minor, lower-priority observations (not counted in the 12):
  code/r_station/process_video_packets.cpp:143 does memcpy(&uRequestId, pPacket
  + sizeof(t_packet_header), sizeof(u32)) with no length check (4-byte OOB read
  for a truncated ACK); code/r_station/rx_video_output.cpp:365 sem_unlink()s
  SEMAPHORE_SM_VIDEO_DATA_AVAILABLE while the player process may still hold it
  open; code/radio/radiolink.c:1330 memcpy's payloadLength (derived from the
  pcap header length) into sPayloadBufferRead[MAX_PACKET_LENGTH_PCAP=4096] with

      330 +### 5.1 What "forwarding / retransmission" means in this syste
          +m                                                             
      331 +It was established from the code, not assumed:                
      332 +                                                              
      333 +- **Retransmission (the link layer).** When a video block is i
          +ncomplete, the                                                
      334 +  station asks the vehicle to send the missing packets again: 
      335 +  `ProcessorRxVideo::checkAndRequestMissingPackets()` builds a
      336 +  `PACKET_TYPE_VIDEO_REQ_MULTIPLE_PACKETS` request (the packet
          + header, the                                                  
      337 +  retransmission id, the video stream index, the flags, the co
          +unt and one                                                   
      338 +  (block index, packet index) pair per missing packet) and put
          +s it in the                                                   
      339 +  **high priority** queue that the radio TX thread reads. The 
          +vehicle parses                                                
      340 +  it (`code/r_vehicle/processor_tx_video.cpp`) and answers wit
          +h the missing                                                 
      341 +  video packets, marked with `PACKET_FLAGS_BIT_RETRANSMITED` a
          +nd                                                            
      342 +  `PACKET_FLAGS_BIT_HIGH_PRIORITY`, with the retransmission id
          + in the video                                                 
      343 +  stream info (`VIDEO_STREAM_INFO_FLAG_RETRANSMISSION_ID`).   
      344 +  The window in which a block is kept for a retransmission is 
      345 +  `Model::getCurrentVideoProfileMaxRetransmissionWindow()`    
      346 +  (`((uProfileEncodingFlags & 0x0000FF00) >> 8) * 5` ms; the d
          +efault                                                        
      347 +  `DEFAULT_VIDEO_RETRANS_MS5_HP` = 14 → **70 ms**). A block th
          +at is older is                                                
      348 +  dropped, not requested.                                     
      349 +- **Forwarding (the output side).** The received video is forw
          +arded to the                                                  
      350 +  local desktop player through the FIFO `/tmp/ruby/fifovideo_d
          +isp`                                                          
      351 +  (`rx_video_output_video_data()` → `_rx_video_output_to_video
          +_streamer_pipe()`),                                           
      352 +  and it can be forwarded further to the UDP port of a local p
          +layer, to an                                                  
      353 +  Ethernet socket (`nVideoForwardETHPort`) or to a USB (tether
          +ing) device.                                                  
      354 +  These are the *output* paths of the station; they are indepe
          +ndent of the                                                  
      355 +  retransmission mechanism and both are now covered: the retra
          +nsmission by                                                  
      356 +  test 14, the FIFO forwarding by the live demonstration of §2
          +.4.                                                           
      357 +

          +top player

       22 +The mission of this session was the primary objective of the p
